title: Lamp of beauty
hook: the Jaap moves into Persian: He is the glorious one, the lamp of beauty (Jaap)

segments.voice: Yesterday, naad, and your line, the dance of dances. Did music move you a little? Today, Jaap changes language in the middle of the hymn. Day three hundred forty-four.

A friend who speaks three languages is telling you a story in English. Then they reach the part they really care about, and suddenly it's Spanish, or Punjabi, or Tagalog. Some things only sound right in one language. Grandma's words. The word for that kind of evening. Partway through Jaap Sahib, the Tenth Guru does something like that. He moves into Persian, the language of poets and courts, and starts talking about beauty. Today: lamp of beauty.
screen: `A FRIEND SWITCHES LANGUAGES.` → `SOME THINGS SOUND RIGHT IN ONE.` → `JAAP SWITCHES INTO PERSIAN.`

segments.voice: In the Tenth Guru's world, Persian was the language of the Mughal court, of government papers, and of a great tradition of love poetry. The Guru knew it well; his letter to the emperor, the Zafarnama, is written in it. So when Jaap moves into Persian and Arabic words, it isn't showing off. It reaches for a language with a long habit of praising beauty. The lines here begin with a little word, ki, meaning something like: for You are. And one of them says the One is husnal charaag. Husn is beauty, the same word Punjabi still uses for a lovely face or a lovely view. Charaag, or chiragh, is a lamp, a small oil lamp of the kind that lit houses and shrines. The lamp of beauty. Think about what that picture does. A lamp isn't beautiful because of its own shape. It's beautiful because it lets you see everything else. Lamplight makes a room golden. So the line suggests that beauty itself has a source, and that every lovely thing is lit by it. In the same Persian stretch, Jaap uses names like kareem, generous, and raheem, merciful, names Muslims also use for God. The Tenth Guru brings them into Sikh morning prayer without hesitating. Jaap reaches for every language the Guru had, Braj, Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, as if to say: no single tongue holds the One, and every tongue can praise.
screen: `PERSIAN: THE LANGUAGE OF COURTS AND POETS.` · `HUSN: BEAUTY. CHARAAG: A LAMP.` · `A LAMP LETS YOU SEE EVERYTHING ELSE.` · `KAREEM AND RAHEEM: SHARED NAMES.` · then, large: `LAMP OF BEAUTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one beautiful thing. Look around you right now and find it. It doesn't have to be grand. The grain in a wooden table. Light on a wall. The curve of a mug handle. Someone's handwriting. Rest your eyes on it. Then notice the light that's letting you see it, a window, a lamp, a screen's glow. The beauty and the light, together. Breathe slowly, and just enjoy it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, the word of wonder. The bell holds the time.
Husnal charaag. Husn is beauty; charaag, a lamp — the One as the lamp that lets every lovely thing be seen.
Your line: makes a room golden. Today, point out one beautiful thing to someone else, out loud, and be the lamp for a second. Day three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Jaap Sahib move through its Persian and Arabic passages each morning in the same rhythm as the rest, and the words husn (beauty) and charaag (lamp) are still familiar in Punjabi.

fork.setup: you want to praise beauty, and you know several languages. which does the Tenth Guru reach for in this stretch of Jaap?
options: Persian, the language of courts and love poetry.
fork.reveal: Jaap switches into Persian and Arabic words here, and calls the One husnal charaag, the lamp of beauty.

original.note: Gurmukhi: husn, beauty, a Persian word still used in Punjabi; Jaap's husnal charaag is the lamp of beauty.

trapdoor: what you thought: the lamp of beauty means God is beautiful.
what it means: like a lamp, the One is the light that lets every beautiful thing be seen.
what a scholar hears: the Persian section uses 'ki … hain' lines with Arabic epithets (kareem, raheem), drawing on the Persianate poetic vocabulary of the Mughal era.

Kareem and raheem appear in Jaap's Persian/Arabic passages (e.g., 'hamesul raheeme', 'kareemul kamaal'): confirm.
